segments.text: Thirty meters down, a diver is pulling bodies out of a sunken tugboat. He reaches for a hand. And the hand grabs him back.
No chance. That boat had been on the sea floor for three days. Nobody lasts three days down there. Let's go look.
May twenty-sixth, {2013|twenty thirteen}. Twenty miles off Nigeria, a tugboat called Jascon Four is holding an oil tanker steady at a platform. Twelve men on board. The sea is rough.
It's before five in the morning. Most of the crew are asleep, doors locked. Out here, you lock your door because of pirates.
The cook, Harrison Okene, twenty-nine, is already up. He's in the bathroom.
Then a swell hits, and the whole boat rolls over. Water punches through the corridors. Minutes later she's upside down on the sea floor.
Harrison is thrown around in total darkness. He feels his way along walls that used to be ceilings, and finds one small space the water hasn't taken. A pocket of air, about four feet high.
The eleven others never got out. The locked doors that kept pirates out kept them in. I don't have a joke for that.
So what does he have? One bottle of Coke. A life vest with two tiny flashlights. That's the whole inventory.
The water is cold enough to kill him in hours. So he drags a mattress over and builds a little platform, just above the surface.
Next problem. Every breath out is carbon dioxide, and the pocket is sealed. A physicist later did the math: that much air buys you about sixty hours.
Then come the noises. Something big, moving through the wreck. He picks up a plank and waits. I'd have lost my mind. And my feathers.
He prays. He thinks about his family. One day goes. Then another. He has no idea how many.
On the third day, he hears an engine. An anchor dropping. Divers, sent down to collect the dead.
Harrison grabs a hammer and pounds on the wall. And the sounds outside fade away. They're leaving.
Then a light slides across the water. A diver is in the corridor, right below him.
So he does the only thing he can. He reaches down into the black water, and takes the diver's hand. The diver screams. Fair.
Then, on the radio, a voice shouts: he's alive!
But they can't just swim him up. After sixty hours at that depth, the surface would kill him. So they warm him with hot water, give him a breathing mask, and bring him up under pressure.
Then more than two days in a decompression chamber, letting the pressure off slowly.
When he finally steps outside, he sees the stars. He thinks he's been gone one day.
About sixty hours at the bottom of the Atlantic. The only survivor. I said no chance. I was wrong. Case closed.
